title: Naraka: Bladepoint
subtitle: On Polyfort Island — Facing a Thousand Years of Craftsmanship in Cold Steel Duels
description: Naraka: Bladepoint is a martial arts-style multiplayer action battle royale game developed by 24 Entertainment Studio under NetEase Games. Players化身 various warriors, competing for survival in cold-weapon combat. But what is most stunning is not the fluid combos and parries — it is that every inch of the battlefield beneath your feet is a meticulous recreation of real heritage architecture. From the terracotta warrior arrays of the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor to the golden-tiled roofs of Wudang Mountains, from the city walls of Pingyao Ancient City to the circular courtyards of Fujian tulou — this article will take you across Naraka's battlefields in search of the thousand-year-old buildings hidden among the flash of blades.

route.title: Naraka: Bladepoint — Seeking a Thousand Years of Heritage on the Cold-Steel Battlefield
route.intro:
Beneath the canopy, all beings are equal
In most competitive games, the 'map' is just the backdrop for fighting. But in Naraka: Bladepoint, the map itself is another main character. When you control Matari leaping from roof to roof, or Yoto Hime running along walls with incredible speed — you think you are 'playing a game,' but you are actually passing through a precisely recreated museum of Chinese ancient architecture. Most notably, the game has a deep collaboration with the Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum. In 2023, Naraka: Bladepoint officially announced a联动 with the museum, bringing the terracotta warriors and Qin dynasty palace architecture into the game scene with极高的精度. This is not a simple borrowing of appearances — the game team obtained field survey data and academic support from the museum, so that every terracotta warrior's hair bun, armor, and facial features in the game have archaeological basis. Let us enter these maps you have fought on countless times — this time, look not at enemies, but at the architecture.

stops.title: Stop 1: Terracotta Warrior Array — The Legion of the Great Qin Rises Anew
stops.content: In Naraka: Bladepoint's 'Morokai' map, there is an underground space that almost every player remembers vividly — in the vast, deep trenches, thousands of clay warrior figures stand densely arrayed. Some hold long spears, others draw bows, others drive chariots — in严整 formation, exuding murderous intent. This scene is a one-to-one digital recreation of the terracotta warrior pits at the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor. The mausoleum of Ying Zheng, the first emperor of China, yielded about eight thousand terracotta figures, clay horses, and chariots from its three accompanying pits, hailed as the 'Eighth Wonder of the World.' Most remarkably, every terracotta warrior's face is unique, as if individually molded from real people rather than produced from molds. In the联动 version, the game team achieved an astonishing level of accuracy in recreating the terracotta warriors. The formation sequence of Pit One — three rows of crossbowmen at the front, one row on each flank, thirty-eight columns of main infantry — is completely preserved. Even the traces of vermilion, mineral green, indigo, and other painted pigments remaining on the warriors are restored in the game textures. These pigments oxidize and flake within minutes of excavation — what we see in museums today are mostly gray 'plain pottery' — but Naraka: Bladepoint boldly restored them to their original colored state. An even more interesting detail: the destructible场景 set in the terracotta pits — the broken pottery fragments and collapsed trenches — are not for 'showing off' but to remind players that the warriors we see today are the result of拼复 after archaeological excavation. The real pits were already大规模 damaged when Xiang Yu entered the Pass, their timber roofs long collapsed and burned. Fighting in such a scene where 'reality and virtual coexist,' every strike feels like battling against two thousand years of time in a fight that can have no victor.

stops.title: Stop 2: Qin Palace Ruins — The Empire's Dream Covering Three Hundred Li
stops.content: Leaving the terracotta pits and ascending, the game scene shifts from 'underground army' to 'above-ground palaces.' In the core area of 'Morokai,' a vast complex modeled on Qin dynasty palace gardens rises from the ground — high platforms, grand roofs, deep eaves, vermilion columns forming solemn colonnades, cloud patterns and chi dragons carved into the阶梯 before the halls. Although there is no direct correspondence to any existing Qin dynasty palace heritage — since no complete above-ground remains of Qin palaces survive — the game team referenced大量 excavation reports of palace foundations through their cooperation with the Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum, as well as Qin dynasty architectural components unearthed in Shaanxi, including tile-ends, hollow bricks, and clay pipes, to extrapolate a scholarly defensible 'Qin palace restoration model.' The layout logic of the building complex, meanwhile, references the spirit of China's most complete and expansive ancient palace city — Wudang Mountains Architecture Complex. Wudang was a royal Daoist site built over twelve years by Ming Emperor Chengzu, including nine palaces and nine temples such as Taihe Palace, Zixiao Palace, and Nanyan Palace. The buildings rise层层 along the mountain地形, perfectly merging the spatial narrative of 'divine right of kings' with natural terrain. The elevated platforms, central axis sequence, and spatial division of front court and rear寝宫 in the game's Qin palace mirror exactly the 'red walls, emerald tiles, and five-tier platforms' of Wudang's Zixiao Palace — only replacing the Daoist immortals with the Qin empire's symbols of the Water Virtue king. Even more admirable is the game team's meticulous考证 of Qin architectural components. The巨大的 kui-dragon patterned tile-ends beneath the palace eaves — nearly half a meter in diameter — their designs taken directly from actual kui-dragon pattern large tile-ends unearthed at the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor. These tile-ends are not merely architectural components but political symbols of the Qin empire's 'Water Virtue kingship.' The dragon and phoenix patterned hollow bricks laid in the halls likewise come from real archaeological finds at the Xianyang Palace site — the game even restores the Qin dynasty 'vermilion painted floor' technique, where cinnabar mixed with tung oil was applied as both a moisture-proof treatment and a silent declaration of imperial majesty. As you roll and dodge across this vermilion floor in the game, you are treading on the real colors of a Qin palace two thousand years ago. When you leap from the platforms of the Qin palace — grappling hook out, running along walls — behind you lies that majestic array of vermilion columns and golden tiles. Setting aside the combat, the architectural impact of this moment alone is worth launching the game.

stops.title: Stop 3: Polyfort Island Gardens — Dueling on the Roofs of Suzhou's Humble Administrator's Garden
stops.content: Moving to the other map 'Polyfort Island' — the style shifts abruptly from the majesty of the Qin empire to the gentleness of Jiangnan. Here lies an extremely refined classical garden area: water dominates the scene, platforms in the water connected by zigzag bridges, Taihu stone rockeries piled on the banks, a corner of flying eaves visible behind the rockeries. If you have even a passing familiarity with Suzhou gardens, you will immediately smile knowingly — is this not the lotus pond outside the Yuanxiang Hall of Humble Administrator's Garden? The Humble Administrator's Garden is Suzhou's largest classical garden, one of China's four great famous gardens, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1997. The entire garden centers on water, with pavilions, terraces, and towers built around it. Yuanxiang Hall is the garden's principal building, named after Zhou Dunyi's phrase 'fragrance spreading far and clear' — north of the hall lies a broad expanse of water, where lotus flowers in summer fill the garden with fragrance. Naraka: Bladepoint choosing to turn this literati garden into an arena is itself a brilliant cultural collision: the Humble Administrator's Garden was designed for 'quiet contemplation' — sitting down for tea, admiring flowers, composing poetry. Naraka: Bladepoint, meanwhile, has warriors running along walls, parrying, and dueling within it. Yet miraculously, this 'violence' does not destroy the garden's beauty — it instead allows players to see the garden from a 'rooftop perspective' for the first time. For those of us who walked properly along the paths of the Humble Administrator's Garden, who would have thought that from the roof of Yuanxiang Hall you could see a different universe? Who would have imagined that beneath the waters of the zigzag bridge lies a perfect ambush point? The game's interaction mechanics (especially the mobility of the flying silk) transform the static garden into a three-dimensional spatial maze — which, to some degree, is actually a 'restoration' of the garden design's original intent: Suzhou gardens were always a 'game of space,' with surprises hidden behind every turn, every lattice window, every rockery. It is just that the ancients played with their feet, while we play with a controller. The next time you are taken down by a combo behind a rockery, do not forget to say: this round was won by the Humble Administrator's Garden.

stops.title: Stop 4: Ancient City Wall — Cold Weapons on the Ramparts of Pingyao
stops.content: At the northern end of the 'Polyfort Island' map, a complete ancient city stands majestically. Tall gray-brick city walls, seventy-two watchtowers spaced along the wall, six heavy arched gates — this is Naraka: Bladepoint's splendid tribute to Pingyao City Wall. Pingyao City Wall was first built in the Western Zhou and expanded in the third year of the Ming Hongwu era (1370). With a circumference of 6,163 meters, it is one of China's four best-preserved ancient city walls and a core component of the UNESCO World Heritage site Pingyao Ancient City. The wall has six barbican gates and seventy-two watchtowers — the number seventy-two symbolizing Confucius's seventy-two disciples, embodying the design philosophy of combining military defense with Confucian教化. The ancient city wall scene in the game perfectly captures the combat essence of Pingyao's walls: the wide top of the wall is broad enough for horsemen; the crenellations are just the right height to cover half the body; the马面 (projecting square platforms) provide flanking fire angles. These were designed in the Ming dynasty to resist Mongol cavalry, and in the game they become natural terrain for grappling hook attachment and ambush sniping. Especially brilliant is the game's use of the 'barbican.' The barbican is a semicircular or square small enclosure outside the city gate — lure the enemy into the barbican, close the two gates, and the defenders rain arrows from the high walls on all sides, like 'catching a turtle in a jar.' In Naraka: Bladepoint, the barbican becomes the most dangerous close-quarters combat arena. With only one exit, if you are trapped inside by three opponents with high walls on all sides, escape is impossible. This design is not凭空 imagined — it is exactly the same logic that Ming defenders used when utilizing barbicans to annihilate attacking forces. The layout of corner towers and马面 on Pingyao City Wall is also precisely reproduced in the game. Corner towers sit at the four corners of the wall, one story higher than the watchtowers, serving as the highest commanding points of the entire defense — in Naraka: Bladepoint, players skilled at long-range sniping will always seize the corner towers first. The马面 (also called敌台) are placed every sixty paces along the wall, projecting several meters outward, allowing defenders to shoot from the flank at enemies scaling the walls. The game sets the spacing of these马面 precisely within the effective range of bows and grappling hooks — the tactical choice of moving from one马面 to the next is the same physical logic that Ming soldiers faced. In other words, the game designers and the Ming dynasty city builders were thinking about the same thing: how to ensure that defenders always have a firepower advantage while on the move. Standing on the ramparts of this virtual ancient city, looking around: seventy-two watchtowers stretch to the horizon in the moonlight. You suddenly remember what Liang Sicheng wrote the first time he stood on Pingyao's city wall — 'This city is the most complete living specimen of an ancient Chinese county town.' And today, this 'specimen' is being traversed by thousands of players with grappling hooks and parried with spears — this may be the coolest way to experience ancient architecture.

stops.title: Stop 5: Tulou Arena — The Circular Courtyard as a Life-or-Death Arena
stops.content: In the southeastern corner of the map, several circular巨构 are scattered among the valleys — huge circular rammed-earth buildings, multiple rings层层叠叠, with a circular courtyard in the center. This is clearly a battlefield adaptation of Fujian Fujian Tulou. Fujian tulou are a UNESCO World Heritage site. The most representative examples include the Nanjing Tianluokeng tulou cluster (one square and four circles, colloquially known as 'four dishes and a soup') and the Hegui Lou, built on a swamp. Tulou are built primarily from raw earth mixed with lime, fine sand, bamboo strips, and other materials, repeatedly pounded and compacted, with walls over two meters thick. Naraka: Bladepoint takes the circular structure of tulou to its extreme — this is a natural 'arena.' The central courtyard is the main stage for combat, and anyone who pokes their head out from the circular corridor is a living target for sniping. And tulou's most essential 'inwardness' — all doors and windows face the courtyard — means that no matter how you move, you are always within your opponent's field of vision. This is perfectly consistent with real tulou defense logic: a tulou is a miniature fortress; once you enter the gate, there is nowhere to hide. Even more brilliant is the game's use of tulou's 'layers' — in a real tulou, the ground floor is the kitchen, the second floor is the granary, and the third and fourth floors are bedrooms, each floor with a different function. The game preserves this layered structure but赋予s it combat significance: the ground-level courtyard is a close-combat zone, the second floor and above are long-range suppression positions, and the top-floor roofs are the aerial corridors for grappling hook players to maneuver and穿插. A complete tulou battle is a three-dimensional military operation — and this 'three-dimensional defense' was precisely the original intent of tulou design. When you are struck by a descending katana from above in the tulou courtyard — do not forget to glance at the sky above. The perfect circle of sky framed by the circular eaves is the same shape that a Hakka grandmother saw three hundred years ago when she looked up while hanging laundry.

stops.title: Stop 6: Dunhuang Apsaras — A Mural Gallery in the Sand and Gravel
stops.content: In Naraka: Bladepoint's 'Morokai' map, there is an area perpetually shrouded in windblown sand. Broken pagodas and grottoes are scattered across the Gobi, their murals weathered yet still revealing the outlines of apsaras and musicians — a poetic tribute to the Mogao Caves of Dunhuang. Mogao Caves (Including the Western Thousand Buddha Caves) is a UNESCO World Heritage site, located on the eastern slope of Mingsha Mountain at the western end of the Hexi Corridor in Dunhuang. Starting from 366 CE (the second year of the Former Qin's Jianyuan era), over a thousand years of carving through ten dynasties created the largest and richest Buddhist art treasury in existence. Today there are 735 caves, 45,000 square meters of murals, and 2,415 colored sculptures. The apsaras of Mogao — those heavenly beings with flowing robes, dancing in the air — are among the most iconic visual symbols in Chinese art history. Naraka: Bladepoint translates the apsara imagery of Dunhuang murals into character动作 language: the posture of a character's lightness skill leaping into the air, the trajectory of a grappling hook in midair, all find their prototypes in the 'apsaras scattering flowers' mural of Mogao Cave 321. And the immensely popular Dunhuang-themed weapon skins — with flowing mineral green and ocher patterns on the blades — originate from the mineral pigments in Mogao murals that have remained vivid for over a millennium. As you chase opponents through the windblown sand of Morokai, passing between crumbling pagodas and skimming over faded murals — this is more than a battle. You are peeling back layers of history's sand, layer by layer, revealing a Buddhist gallery that has been buried by the wind and sand for far too long.
